Accommodation is most likely when the episode is treated as credible information and updating is psychologically safe: low to moderate threat, high legitimacy (the source or process is competent, fair, informed, and relevant), and high belonging security (updating is unlikely to jeopardize acceptance in a valued group). Larger and clearer discrepancies then increase pressure to update, and repeated discrepancies under stable conditions further increase accommodation. Concretely, accommodation is favored when an individual can treat the episode as a "hard truth" delivered by a credible source in a context that does not threaten belonging security (e.g., role-skill learning after specific, fair feedback from a trusted teammate; cultural or personal learning after a meaningful narrative episode; practice-level learning when a respected outsider engages gamers respectfully).

Assimilation is most likely when the mismatch is treated as insufficiently diagnostic to justify updating, but not so threatening that it must be actively fought. Assimilation is favored by small, ambiguous, or low-clarity discrepancies (mixed signals, uncertain causes), low personal relevance (the episode does not touch valued standards), low stakes, or low perceived potency (the episode feels like a one-off). It can also be favored under moderate threat when an easy reframe is available: the discrepancy produces discomfort, but the individual preserves the current identity state by explaining the episode away without escalating into defensive conflict. The practical stance is: "This does not really tell me anything new about who I am or who we are." This can be rational when the episode is plausibly noisy or unrepresentative (e.g., losing due to lag or trolling; discounting a teammate's complaint as tilt rather than informative feedback; minimizing a mild stereotype cue when there is no consequential audience and it can be shrugged off).

Antagonism is most likely when the discrepancy is processed as identity-threatening and "learning" is experienced as conceding to an illegitimate or hostile frame. It is favored by high threat (devaluation, stigma, humiliation, exclusion risk, moral accusation), low legitimacy (the evaluator is seen as biased, ignorant, or outgrouphostile), and low or precarious belonging security. Publicness or audience pressure further pushes toward antagonism because reputation is at stake. Under this configuration, large discrepancies and repeated negative feedback do not necessarily produce learning pressure but can amplify defensive escalation, because the system treats the episode as evidence of hostility rather than evidence about the self. This is especially relevant at the practice layer when gamer identity is central and boundaries are salient (e.g., public discourse portraying gamers as morally suspect, experienced as contemptuous or unin-formed, increases boundary salience and moralized defense). Analogous dynamics occur at the social layer (sanctions reinterpreted as illegitimate exercises of authority) and cultural layer (mainstream framings interpreted as moral panic). Uncertainty-identity theory offers a complementary account of why this configuration is stabilizing, holding that self-uncertainty increases the appeal of clearly bounded, highly distinctive groups and of their normative prescriptions (Hogg, 2007).

These dynamics indicate that resolution is driven by the interaction of threat with legitimacy and belonging security (see Figure 6): low threat with high legitimacy and high belonging security favors accommodation; low threat with low legitimacy or low belonging security favors assimilation; high threat with low legitimacy and low belonging security favors antagonism; and high threat with high legitimacy and high belonging security can yield mixed outcomes but often permits accommodation when the individual feels secure enough to treat the feedback as a costly but credible signal.

Because the same moderators can take different values for different layers, resolution is layer-specific within the same episode (e.g., personal accommodation alongside practice antagonism).

A central contribution of the framework is that resolution need not be singular or uniform across layers. The same episode can yield different resolution modes across identity layers, producing a resolution profile rather than a single outcome. For example, an individual may accommodate at the personal layer ("I need to manage frustration"), assimilate at the social layer ("my teammates were unfair"), and antagonize at the practice layer ("the criticism of gamers is biased and stigmatizing"), even when the same person acknowledges their own irritability while rejecting generalized claims about gamers as illegitimate. This layer-specific structure clarifies why individuals can appear open to learning in one respect and defensive in another within the same event. The family-dinner example in Figure 7 illustrates that the same event can be appraised against four different reference points (the self, the ingroup role, the cultural frame, and gamer identity as a category), each yielding its own discrepancy, moderator profile, and resolution mode.

One implication is that similar discrepancy profiles can yield identity updating for one individual and defensive polarization for another, depending on perceived threat, perceived legitimacy, and belonging security, and on prior identity centrality and boundary salience. This provides a mechanism for why exposure-based "effects" studies often produce inconsistent outcomes across samples, contexts, and historical eras: as the distribution of perceived threat, security, and legitimacy shifts, the dominant resolution mode shifts accordingly, altering whether episodes are metabolized as learning, discounted as noise, or converted into defensive strengthening.

Step 6: Updating

In Step 6, the episode's information is translated into an immediate, preliminary update of the identity structure. This is the framework's principal structural revision: the episode updates personal, social, cultural, and practicebased gamer identity simultaneously, and changes in one layer can directly shape changes in another within the same episode. Identity is therefore not updated one layer at a time.

Step 6 produces a provisional post-episode identity state: the "working version" of who the person now takes themselves to be (personally, socially, culturally, and as a gamer) immediately after the episode. This updated state carries forward into the next episode as a starting condition, shaping subsequent selection, salience, and interpretation. Identity change depends on two separable conditions. First, the episode must be good evidence for a given layer (i.e., counted for that layer rather than trivial or noisy), shaped by diagnosticity (potency in Step 4). Second, the person must be willing and able to incorporate that evidence rather than explain it away or treat it as a threat, shaped by learnability (resolution in Step 5). Potency therefore tells us how much the episode could change identity in that layer; resolution tells us whether it will, and in what direction.

A highly diagnostic episode can still produce little change if it is not treated as learnable, and a strong mismatch does not guarantee learning when processed as illegitimate or hostile. Magnitude and direction of change are further constrained by the cap, which operates at the level of each layer rather than as a single budget across layers: each layer has its own upper bound on how much change a single episode can produce, independent of the other layers. Step 6 combines realized potency and resolution into an effective update per layer (see Figure 8): • If potency is low, the episode cannot move identity much in that layer even when the individual is open to learning.

• If potency is high but discrepancy is resolved via assimilation, the layer remains largely stable.

• If potency is high and resolution is accommodation, change is stronger and directionally consistent with the discrepancy signal.

• If potency is high and resolution is antagonism, change can still occur but in a defensive direction (boundary salience, moralization, distrust of the source, or counter-updating).

The result is an immediate update to the identity state across all relevant layers, producing a provisional configuration that reflects the episode's discrepancy signals filtered through potency, resolution, affect, meaning, and the cap.

Personal self-schemas can shift (e.g., "I am competent," "I am impulsive," "I am fair") depending on personal discrepancies and whether accommodation occurs. Commit- ment and uncertainty also adjust, typically more slowly, reflecting whether the person feels more settled or more exploratory afterward. A public failure in a valued skill domain may increase uncertainty ("maybe I'm not who I thought"), unless it is assimilated ("bad luck") or antagonized ("the evaluation was unfair"). Sustained questioning of an existing commitment corresponds to reconsideration of commitment, one of the three dimensions in the identity model of Crocetti et al. (2008).

Identification with a relevant group can strengthen or weaken depending on belonging, sanctions, recognition, and resolution. Role-related components can shift as well (e.g., "I fit this role," "I am a core member," "this group is not for me"). Being publicly praised by a guild for leadership, when social potency is high and resolution favors accommodation, can increase identification and perceived prototypicality.

Cultural identification and its linked meanings can strengthen or weaken depending on legitimacy, ritual framing, and perceived coherence of the episode with the cultural narrative, including whether the person treats the frame as meaningful and self-relevant going forward. A highly ritualized esports event that feels legitimate and emotionally meaningful can strengthen cultural identification with that scene.

Practice-based gamer identity can update along several components, including how self-defining "being a gamer" feels (gamer centrality), whether gaming is experienced as reliably delivering competence, belonging, meaning, and distinctiveness (accumulated need satisfaction), how accessible and important gamer vs. non-gamer distinctions become (boundary salience), and whether gamer identity becomes more morally defended and normatively demanding (moralization). A stigmatizing public confrontation about gamers may not change how a person plays, but it can increase boundary salience and moralization through antagonistic resolution.

A distinctive feature of the framework is that the four identity layers do not update independently. They can be coupled within the same episode, such that shifts in one layer amplify or dampen shifts in another. Coupling can be integrative or conflictual.

Integrative coupling occurs when updates align across layers and mutually reinforce. Defending games in a public professional setting, for example, can simultaneously generate practice-layer signals (enactment and boundary management), social-layer signals (respect from valued peers and status-relevant recognition), and cultural-layer signals (gaming framed as legitimate culture). When resolution favors accommodation, these converging signals can jointly increase gamer identity centrality and consolidation likelihood more than any one channel alone. Similarly, social recognition and cultural legitimacy can amplify practice identity centrality and, in some cases, moralization.

Conflictual coupling occurs when updates are misaligned across layers and therefore reduce consolidation or redirect restructuring. A person may experience strong The lower panel plots the four layer-specific discrepancies within a two-dimensional resolution space defined by perceived threat (vertical axis) and perceived legitimacy and belonging security (horizontal axis, combined because they jointly determine whether updating is safe and warranted). In this example, personal and social discrepancies fall in the accommodation zone, while cultural and gamer discrepancies fall in the antagonism zone, illustrating that the same episode can produce a mixed resolution profile across identity layers. belonging in a gamer group (a strong social signal) but evaluate community norms as inconsistent with personal moral standards or broader values (personal or cultural discrepancy). Under these conditions, practice identity consolidation may be weakened even in a highengagement episode, or the system may shift toward later restructuring rather than straightforward consolidation. How much cross-layer misalignment a person can absorb should depend in part on self-complexity, because greater differentiation among self-aspects limits the spillover of negative feedback from one domain into others (Linville, 1985 (Linville, , 1987)).

Consider a high-potency, high-opportunity episode such as a major competitive event or a public debate about gaming. The same episode can simultaneously generate personal signals (e.g., "I performed well under pressure," "I failed my self-standard"), social signals (e.g., "my group accepted and praised me," "I was sanctioned"), cultural signals (e.g., "this is a legitimate cultural ritual," "this frame feels incoherent or devaluing"), and practicebased gamer signals (e.g., "being a gamer is publicly recognized," "gamers are disrespected here"). If resolution favors accommodation, these signals reinforce one another, increasing identity centrality and the likelihood of consolidation. If resolution favors antagonism (e.g., the episode is framed through hostile outgroup discourse), the practice-layer update may shift toward boundary hardening and moralization even while personal competence and social-role competence strengthen. The framework therefore predicts mixed, coupled outcomes within the same episode.

Step 7: Stabilization

The provisional identity state from Step 6 does not automatically become the lasting carryover identity state. Step 6 can update multiple layers at once, sometimes in different directions, leaving the post-episode state temporarily workable but internally tense, or meaningful but not durable. Step 7 therefore introduces two slower processes that shape what endures: coherence regulation (Step 7a), which makes the configuration internally consistent enough to function, and consolidation (Step 7b), which determines which episodes and identity shifts become stable reference points for future episodes. After joint updating in Step 6, the identity configuration may contain contradictions across beliefs, norms, and identifications because different layers were updated in parallel. In Step 7a, identity elements tend to become coherent enough to function over time, consistent with classic consistency traditions (e.g., cognitive dissonance, balance logic). Coherence regulation operates as pressure for cognitive balance: not a single conscious choice but a gradual corrective pull that reduces tension among linked identity elements through belief revision, boundary adjustment, and meaning redefinition.

A simple example illustrates the kind of tension that can arise after Step 6: a person may simultaneously hold "I value inclusivity," "real gamers are exclusionary," and "I am a real gamer." Without coherence regulation, identity systems could accumulate contradictions indefinitely. Coherence regulation prevents this through selective adjustment: some elements become anchors while others adjust to support a workable self-narrative. Coherence regulation typically does not erase the episode's updates but rearranges how they fit together, often through revising what the identity implies (e.g., redefining "real gamer" standards), narrowing or redrawing category boundaries, or altering which norms are treated as central. When contradictions arise, adjustment tends to occur first in the most flexible elements, while more entrenched commitments are less likely to change.

Coherence alone does not determine what becomes influential over time. Step 7b introduces consolidation

as a selective stabilization process that determines which episodes and identity shifts persist; not all episodes are retained equally. Consolidation refers to the process by which certain episodes become more rehearsed, easier to put into words, and more likely to be stored as memories that feel identity-defining, effectively becoming "narrative chapters" in one's identity (McAdams, 1993). Work on autobiographical reasoning describes this process in more detail, showing how individuals link specific events to a wider life story and draw self-relevant conclusions from them (Habermas & Bluck, 2000; Pasupathi et al., 2007). Consolidation is more likely when episodes are high in potency, identity salience, public consequence, and emotional meaning. Consolidation probability is therefore a downstream function of realized potency from Step 4: the same factors that make an episode identity-diagnostic during appraisal also make its resulting identity shifts more likely to persist as stable reference points. These episodes become easier to retrieve, and they shape the next cycle more strongly than less consolidated episodes do, by influencing future episode selection ( Step 0

) and which identity lenses become salient (Step 1).

This selective consolidation has downstream consequences for boundary dynamics. Repeated public stigma episodes (high opportunity, high practice salience) can consolidate into an identity narrative such as "outsiders do not understand gamers," such that repetition combined with consolidation gradually increases boundary salience and moralization over time. Conversely, repeated recognition episodes can consolidate into a different narrative such as "I am the kind of gamer who supports others," for example when mentoring newcomers is socially valued and becomes a rehearsed, identity-defining chapter that shapes both personal self-schemas (e.g., being helpful or prosocial) and practice-based gamer identity in mutually reinforcing ways.

Loop Closure

After coherence regulation and consolidation, the updated identity configuration becomes the starting condition for the next episode, closing the recursive loop: identity shapes selection and salience; episodes shape identity through appraisal, resolution, and coupled updating; coherence regulation and consolidation shape what remains internally workable and what becomes retrievable; and the cycle repeats. Concretely, the carryover state includes the person's current personal self-schemas and commitments, their pattern of group identifications and role expectations, their cultural identifications and associated meanings, and their practice-based gamer identity (centrality, accumulated need satisfaction, boundary salience, moralization). Because Step 7 selectively stabilizes some changes and allows others to fade, the carryover state is not simply the immediate post-episode update from Step 6 but the version of that update coherent enough to function and durable enough to influence future processing.

This loop closure has direct implications for how the framework explains continuity and change. Behavior and experience can look stable even when episodes vary because stable carryover identity configurations constrain selection ( Step 0

), salience activation (Step 1), and discrepancy extraction (Step 4).

Change can be nonlinear: when episodes consistently deliver similar discrepancy signals under high potency and a resolution profile that permits learning, coupled updating can gradually shift multiple identity layers, and consolidation can make those shifts increasingly persistent. Conversely, when episodes are repeatedly resolved through assimilation, even high-potency discrepancies may fail to generate durable change; when repeatedly resolved through antagonism, change can occur in a defensive direction (especially at the practice-based gamer layer), making boundary salience and moralization more stable and increasingly likely to shape later interpretation.

This loop closure also clarifies how the framework explains path dependence as something that builds up through repeated episode cycles rather than as a special case (see Figure 9). Episodes that become well retained through consolidation are easier to recall than most and can steer the next cycle by shaping which episodes are entered (Step 0), how opportunity is interpreted and acted upon (Step 3), and how ambiguous cues are appraised and resolved (Steps 4 and 5). Early differences in identity configuration, access to high-opportunity contexts, or exposure to recognition versus stigma episodes can therefore accumulate into systematically different episode streams and identity trajectories over months and years, even when individuals have similar overall gaming time. Step 7 thus functions as the bridge between within-episode dynamics and longer-term identity development: it determines which short-term updates become part of the person's stable carryover identity state, and therefore which aspects of the cycle become self-reinforcing over time. The need to specify how processes unfolding in real time aggregate into change over developmental time is a central requirement for identity theory generally (Lichtwarck-Aschoff et al., 2008).

Discussion

Summary and Integration

In this paper, we proposed a fundamental reconceptualization of how gaming is theorized in psychological research. Rather than treating video games as static stimuli whose effects can be captured through simple exposure metrics, we have argued that gaming is best understood as an identity-relevant, socially embedded, and historically evolving practice. The appropriate object of study is therefore not game content or hours played in isolation, but the person-in-context: the kinds of gaming episodes individuals enter, the identities they bring into those episodes, the feedback they receive, and how those episodes recursively reshape identity over time.

This reconceptualization is a construct-level contribution. A substantial share of gaming research has relied on undifferentiated exposure variables (e.g., "violent video game exposure," "total play time," "genre classification") even though the same nominal game can instantiate markedly different psychological realities depending on whether the player is engaged in solitary story progression, competitive ranked performance, team coordination, sandbox creativity, public identity enactment, or cultur-ally meaningful participation. Collapsing these experiences into a single variable obscures the mechanisms linking gaming to psychological outcomes and yields heterogeneous findings, weak generalizability, temporally bound claims, and recommendations that do not map onto what gaming actually is. A structurally parallel problem has been identified for identity conflict at work, where a proliferation of competing labels and ad hoc measures was argued to impede the accumulation of knowledge and to render quantitative synthesis largely infeasible (Vough et al., 2025). The framework's relevance scales with the extent to which the phenomenon under study is identity-relevant, socially embedded, historically extended, or shaped by prior episode selection and construal.

The paper proceeded through cumulative stages. First, a historically informed narrative review documented how gaming evolved from simple arcade entertainment into persistent, socially networked, culturally consequential ecosystems. This served a specific theoretical function: establishing that the scientific object "video games" has changed so substantially over five decades that theories calibrated to earlier forms risk becoming temporally stale. Early arcade games were brief, mechanically straightforward, and relatively low in narrative depth; home consoles expanded duration and narrative engagement; the 1990s and 2000s introduced far greater mechanical, perceptual, and cognitive complexity; and recent decades have further transformed games into persistent service platforms, social infrastructures, and cultural ecosystems that intersect with streaming, education, fandom, esports, and mainstream media. The construct of "video game exposure" no longer refers to a stable, well-bounded stimulus: a modern video game can be a social role, a reputational arena, a symbolic universe, or a continuously accessible community.

Second, a conceptual analysis established the identity functions gaming now serves, identifying four levels of contribution. At the personal level, gaming provides a structured yet flexible context for exploration, selfschema formation, competence experiences, moral experimentation, and narrative self-construction. At the social level, it is a site of group membership, role differentiation, norm learning, coordination, sanctions, reputation, and parasocial belonging. At the cultural level, it is a source of master narratives, shared symbols, rituals, language, public events, and transmedia cultural codes, with emphasis on heterogeneity rather than a monolithic "gaming culture." At the practice-based level, "gamer" itself can become a self-defining identity: not merely a preference label but a meta-identity anchored in repeated participation across the gaming ecology, supported by need satisfaction, public recognition, boundary salience, and moralization.

Third, and most centrally, these conceptual insights were formalized into an integrative, episode-based framework specifying a recursive cycle linking gaming and identity. The framework treats episodes (i.e., bounded units of experience in which gaming or gamer identity is meaningfully implicated) as the fundamental unit of analysis, and specifies a multi-step process through which identities carry into episodes ( Step The core thesis is that gaming and identity are mutually constitutive across repeated episodes. Identity shapes what gaming-related situations people enter, how they interpret them, and how they behave within them; those episodes generate identity-relevant feedback that is appraised, resolved, and selectively stabilized, producing updated personal, social, cultural, and gamer identities that influence future episodes. This claim integrates the historical observation that the phenomenon has changed, the conceptual observation that gaming now serves multiple identity functions simultaneously, and the mechanistic specification of how those functions operate dynamically over time.

Fourth, the theoretical and practical implications of this framework are now considered. These are drawn from the framework's internal logic and its relationship to existing research practices, and clarify what the model changes about how gaming is studied, interpreted, and discussed.

Theoretical Implications

From "Exposure" to "Recursive Person-in-Episode Systems"

The first and most fundamental implication is that the framework changes the basic causal ontology of video game research. The relevant causal object is no longer "video game exposure" conceived as an external input acting on a passive recipient. It is a recursive personin-episode system in which identity enters the episode as a carryover state, shapes selection, framing, salience, interpretation, and behavior, and is then updated by appraisal, resolution, and stabilization. The model therefore replaces a linear exposure-to-outcome logic with a feedback system: the person is partly generating the very experiences that later appear to "affect" them (Ashforth & Schinoff, 2016).

This shift has important consequences for what counts as a valid explanation. A gaming outcome at any given time is the result of prior stabilized identity, prior episode selection, prior interpretations, and prior consolidation, not simply the current episode. Many outcomes studied in gaming research are therefore historically produced states rather than immediate reactions to proximal content, so any explanation treating an outcome as a straightforward consequence of recent exposure is incomplete. This applies most forcefully to research questions where identity, social embeddedness, or prior selection are plausibly operative; for narrower questions about immediate cognitive or perceptual effects of well-bounded tasks, standard experimental logic may remain more defensible.

Endogeneity as a Constitutive Property of the Phenomenon

The framework defines episode exposure as endogenous: individuals do not encounter episodes randomly but select into them based on motives, self-concept match, group ties, anticipated meaning, habit, and expected need satisfaction. Observed associations between gaming and identity-relevant outcomes therefore cannot be cleanly interpreted as pure effects of gaming, because exposure is partly produced by prior identity. In causal language, the model implies selection into treatment followed by treatment-induced changes in later selection. The claim "playing video games causes X" becomes theoretically incomplete unless one also specifies who selected which episode stream, under what identity configuration, and why.

Endogeneity is not a methodological nuisance to be controlled away but a constitutive feature of the phenomenon, in contrast to process accounts of identity that specify recursive feedback loops yet still treat endogeneity as a design threat to be addressed with longitudinal data and third variables (Vough et al., 2025). The recursive loop through which identity shapes episode selection and episodes reshape identity is precisely the mechanism the framework describes; removing endogeneity from the system would remove the phenomenon itself. Video game research therefore cannot simply aim to "control for selection" as if selection were a confound external to the process: selection is internal to the process.

This raises a question about ecological validity. In a laboratory design, the experimenter determines which game participants play and for how long, and does so in an environment that often bears little resemblance to settings in which players typically engage with games. How closely does this approximate the experience of a player who selects a personally owned game, chooses when to play, and does so in a familiar environment? Within the exposure-based tradition, such designs are considered adequate, because the primary variable of interest is the stimulus itself. The present framework suggests this level of specification is insufficient. This does not imply that experimental approaches are inappropriate; rather, it indicates that greater attention is required to sampling strategies, experimental paradigms, and analytical models that can accommodate the complexity of the gaming-identity process.

Layered Reciprocal Effects

The framework specifies reciprocity at a finer grain than the general claim that gaming affects identity and identity affects gaming. The effects are distributed across four identity layers (personal, social, cultural, and gamer identity) that can be activated and updated in parallel, with updates in one layer amplifying or dampening updates in another, a structural logic paralleled in intrapersonal identity network research, in which mutually enhancing ties between self-representations allow their motivational effects to spread while conflicting or absent ties prevent that spread (Strauss et al., 2026). Reciprocal effects are therefore multidimensional and can be internally mixed: the same episode can produce personal learning, social repositioning, cultural defensiveness, and gamer-identity hardening simultaneously. The framework therefore rejects the expectation that a single episode should yield a single global direction of change.

This has an important consequence: inconsistent findings across studies may reflect not noise or poor methodology but the genuine multidimensionality of the process, paralleling the argument in the replication literature that variation in findings across samples is frequently misdiagnosed as non-replicability when it in fact reflects non-generalizability arising from unrecognized boundary conditions (Moeller et al., 2025). A study measuring only personal-level outcomes may detect learning, while a study measuring only practice-level outcomes in the same context may detect defensiveness. Both are valid observations of a single process that produces mixed layer-specific profiles. "Mixed" here refers to the possibility that the same episode can have different implications for the person as an individual, for a specific ingroup role, for the cultural frame, and for gamer identity as a superordinate category, and that these levels can move in different directions within the same event. The framework therefore predicts that apparent contradictions in the literature can sometimes be resolved by recognizing that different studies indexed different layers of a multi-layered response.

Path Dependence and Nonlinear Development

Because the updated and stabilized identity state becomes the starting condition for the next episode, the framework implies path dependence and therefore nonstationarity: a process estimated for a given person over one period need not hold for that same person in another, which is why person-specific models have been extended to allow time-varying parameters (Kuper et al., 2025). Early differences in identity configuration, access to particular gaming contexts, stigma exposure, or social recognition can accumulate into systematically different episode streams and therefore different developmental trajectories, even when total gaming time is similar. Heterogeneity in outcomes is therefore not residual variance that sits outside the theory; it is predicted by the theory.

The framework further implies that change should often be nonlinear. Self-reinforcing trajectories emerge when episodes consistently deliver similar discrepancy signals under conditions favoring accommodation, gradually shifting multiple identity layers and making those shifts increasingly persistent. Conversely, repeated assimilation produces apparent inertia in which even highpotency discrepancies fail to generate durable change, while repeated antagonistic resolution produces defensive drift, especially at the practice-based gamer layer, so that boundary salience and moralization become increasingly stable and increasingly likely to redirect subsequent interpretation and selection. Average effects across heterogeneous samples should therefore often appear weak or inconsistent because the underlying process is recursive and path-dependent, and a group-level average need not describe the response pattern of even a simple majority of the persons sampled (McManus et al., 2023).

Redefining What Counts as an "Effect"

Under this framework, an effect is not limited to direct content-driven change. A consequential effect can occur through selection, salience, defensive resolution, or consolidation. Public stigma may not change gameplay behavior directly, for example, but it may increase boundary salience, distrust, and moralization at the gamer-identity layer, which then changes how future episodes are interpreted and which episodes are entered. That is still an effect in the framework: a second-order, recursive, identitymediated effect that would be invisible to a study measuring only direct behavioral change from a proximal manipulation.

This broadens the theoretical map of causal relevance considerably. Out-of-game episodes, public discourse, family conflict, institutional stigma, and recognition by valued audiences all become part of the causal ecology, so video game research cannot remain confined to in-game content if it aspires to explain person-level change. Many effects are also historically distributed rather than punctual: a later reaction may be attributable not to the immediate event alone but to the chain connecting prior gaming-derived meaning to current construal, appraisal, and resolution. Many real-life outcomes conventionally described as "effects of video games" are more accurately described as historically mediated effects that travel through memory, meaning, and identity organization.

The Pivot of Change: Discrepancy Plus Resolution

The framework implies that identity change depends on two separable conditions: whether an episode is potent enough to produce interpretable evidence, and whether the person treats that evidence as something to learn from rather than dismiss or defend against. High-impact episodes do not guarantee learning; they may instead produce assimilation or antagonism, depending on perceived threat, legitimacy, and belonging security.

This implies a more nuanced theory of reciprocal effects in which reciprocity is mediated by interpretive regulation: the episode does not mechanically inscribe itself into identity but must first survive threat, legitimacy, and belonging-security filters. This explains why the same nominal event can produce growth in one person and defensive polarization in another, and implies that any effort to change gaming-related identity outcomes must attend not only to the content of episodes but to the conditions under which they are processed.

Episodes as Psychologically Constituted: A Constrained Constructivist Position

A further implication emerges from the framework's treatment of episodes. The framework defines out-of-game episodes as real-life encounters that activate episodic memory or semantic knowledge developed within video games, and it states that any real-life situation can count as an episode if it satisfies the boundedness criteria and the social information processed in it shares some connection with video games in the individual's mind. Whether a situation qualifies as an episode is therefore not an intrinsic property of the situation but a relation between person and situation. The same dinner conversation, classroom debate, work conflict, or public criticism may be an episode for one person and not for another, depending on whether gaming-derived meaning is activated.

This represents an ontological shift from traditional theories. In conventional approaches, researchers classify events first and then ask what effects they have; in this framework, classification itself is partly psychologically generated. The model therefore goes further than acknowledging that people react to episodes differently: people partly construct what counts as an episode. This shifts the framework from an event ontology to a transactional ontology, where the real unit is not the external situation alone but the relation between the situation and the participant's meaning system, an ontological commitment shared by network approaches to the self-concept, in which the tie between two self-representations is a property of the person's perception rather than of the representations themselves (Strauss et al., 2026).

This adds a second layer of endogeneity beyond selection endogeneity. Even after a situation occurs, the person partly generates whether it counts as a gamingrelevant episode by processing it through gaming-derived semantic and identity traces. People thus partly produce the situations they enter (selection endogeneity) and partly produce the psychological status of the situations they encounter (construal endogeneity). The framework therefore encompasses both self-selection into environments and self-selection into interpretations.

Several downstream consequences follow. First, the ingame or real-life distinction becomes analytically weak: the same recursive machinery operates in both contexts whenever gamer identity, gaming scripts, stigma, legitimacy, or boundary cues are active. Gaming functions as a distributed ecology of meaning rather than a bounded leisure activity, and the recursive cycle need not pause between sessions: family conflicts, classroom discussions, or public stereotype cues can reactivate gaming-linked meanings and continue the cycle through ordinary daily life. Second, the framework predicts both within-person expansion and between-person variability. Path dependence may be self-expanding within a person, with consolidated gaming-related memories and meanings rendering a growing range of later situations amenable to gaming-relevant interpretation. Across persons, individuals differ not only in how they respond to episodes but in which events constitute episodes, so two people can inhabit the same objective social world yet live in different psychological episode ecologies.

The most far-reaching conceptual consequence is that the framework ceases to be a theory of the effects of video games as objects and becomes a theory of identitymediated meaning transfer from video games into lived experience: gaming is not merely something people do but part of how situations are segmented, appraised, narrated, and linked to identity.

These features place the framework within a constructivist theoretical tradition, though a constrained one. The framework is constructivist in three senses: situations become episodes through the participant's meaning-making, not merely through objective event properties; identity change follows a logic of discrepancy, appraisal, and accommodation or antagonism aligned with developmental constructivist thinking; and cultural identity, legitimacy, stigma, and public narratives are socially produced before being internalized and reactivated within episodes. The model nonetheless retains structural opportunity, feasibility constraints, publicness, sanctions, feedback clarity, legitimacy, and limits on single-episode change magnitude. The best characterization is therefore a transactional constructivism: meaning is actively constructed, but construction is constrained by social structure, material affordances, audiences, feedback, and prior identity organization.

Convergence With Critiques of Causal Inference in Technology Research

The framework's implications converge with recent critiques of causal inference in technology-related psychological research and, more broadly, with cross-disciplinary assessments of what can and cannot be causally identified about human behavior (Bailey et al., 2024). Bak-Coleman (2025) has argued that, for social media, individual-level randomized controlled trials often cannot yield coherent causal estimates because the treatment cannot be isolated at the individual level: one person's outcome depends on others' use, on the broader media environment, and on prior societal changes produced by platforms. The present framework supports a structurally analogous argument for video games, though with different mechanisms.

Both arguments challenge the assumption of a self-contained exposure. For social media, the problem is primarily network interference and environmental spillover: the treatment spreads through social ties, institutions, and the broader ecology, so that untreated individuals are still indirectly exposed. For video games, the problem is primarily interpretive and developmental spillover: the psychologically relevant exposure extends beyond explicit gameplay because gaming-derived meanings, schemas, identities, and memories can be reactivated in later nongame situations, while identity simultaneously shapes which situations are entered and how they are construed. This similarity is strongest for multiplayer and teambased games, live-service ecosystems, esports and streaming, gaming communities and fandoms, identity threat and stigma processes, and transmedia franchises, contexts in which one person's gaming outcome depends on others' participation, public meaning systems, and broader cultural frames. Both critiques reject the assumption that exposure can be treated as a stable, externally bounded input, but for different reasons: one because the exposure is socially distributed across people, the other because the exposure is psychologically distributed across episodes, meanings, and identity-linked construals across time. The present framework identifies two further sources of causal complexity beyond network interference: endogeneity of episode selection and the participant-constituted nature of episode status. The treatment is thus both socially nonisolable and psychologically non-fixed.

Importantly, this critique applies most forcefully when gaming is conceptualized broadly (i.e., as a socially embedded, identity-relevant practice) and when the research question concerns broad outcomes such as identity development, societal integration and social functioning, or psychosocial adjustment. For narrower questions about the short-term effects of playing a fixed offline game for a defined period on an immediately measured cognitive or affective outcome, individual-level experimental designs may remain more defensible (provided the endogeneity problem is adequately addressed). Our framework preserves this distinction by differentiating private, high-salience but low-opportunity episodes from public, high-opportunity ones. We do not claim that randomized experiments can never identify causal effects of gaming, which would overreach our framework's logic, but we believe that, for broad questions about gaming as an identity-relevant, socially embedded practice, individuallevel treatment contrasts can misspecify the causal object and may violate key assumptions because the phenomenon is socially distributed, version-unstable, and extended beyond discrete play, with version instability instantiating the general consistency problem in which a cause that can be realized in multiple ways with differing downstream consequences does not define a well-posed causal question (Bailey et al., 2024).

Novel Perspectives: Three Brief Illustrations

In order to make the general implications elaborated above more concrete, we briefly illustrate the framework's application to three debates in which video games are prominent. In each case the framework is reinterpretive and integrative rather than replacement-oriented: it does not discard existing theories but relocates them within a recursive, identity-mediated episode ecology, and its incremental value scales with how identity-relevant, socially embedded, and recursively selected the phenomenon under study is. Appraisal theory has been put to the same integrative use in the literature on identity conflict at work, where theories developed for other purposes had previously been applied piecemeal to separate stages of a single process (Vough et al., 2025).

Endogeneity and the Violent Video Game Debate.

The relationship between violent video games (VVGs) and aggression has been among the most contested questions in psychological science for three decades. The literature is organized around two camps: one reporting reliable, but modest, effects of violent content (Anderson et al., 2010; Anderson & Bushman, 2018), the other claiming negligible or null effects and attributing positive findings to artifact and bias (Ferguson, 2015; Hilgard et al., 2017; Hilgard et al., 2019). Beneath the dispute over effect sizes lies a more basic disagreement over causal interpretation: whether observed associations reflect a causal effect of violent content within video games or the selfselection of more aggressive individuals into VVGs (Bushman & Whitaker, 2010; Elson & Ferguson, 2014). The dominant theoretical tools, principally the General Aggression Model (GAM; Anderson & Bushman, 2018) and, for enactment, the I³ framework (Finkel, 2014), treat violent content as the causal input and aggression as the output, with self-selection handled as a confound to be controlled away.

Our framework's most consequential contribution here follows from endogeneity. If exposure to episodes is partly generated by prior identity rather than externally imposed, then the two positions that structure the debate, "VVGs cause aggression" and "aggressive people choose VVGs," are not rival hypotheses to be adjudicated but two moments of a single recursive process. Consistent with our framework's Step 0 (Selection), prior identity configurations shape which episode streams a person enters; those episodes update identity states through appraisal and resolution (Steps 4 and 5); and the updated states shape subsequent selection. Selection into treatment and treatment-induced change in later selection are therefore interleaved, and the received question (i.e., "is it a true effect or is it selection?") is revealed as a false dichotomy rather than an empirical contest with a single winner. Endogeneity is not a nuisance to be purged; removing it would remove the phenomenon the framework describes.

This reframing accommodates features of the literature that the exposure logic can only treat as noise. Persistent heterogeneity in effect sizes is expected rather than anomalous. Players differ systematically in the motives and preferences they bring to play (Hilgard et al., 2013). Two players with identical play time may therefore occupy different episode ecologies, such as a high-salience, high-opportunity ranked competition versus a low-salience solo session, and diverge in aggressionrelevant consequences for reasons the framework specifies. And study reactivity is reconceived from a methodological artifact into a substantive process: because taking part in a study that is visibly about "the effects of violent video games" is itself an out-of-game episode, it can activate gamer identity, and, among gamers, an evaluative framing can trigger antagonistic resolution that alters the very responses the study intends to measure (Greitemeyer, 2014; Seetahul & Greitemeyer, 2024; see also Seetahul & Greitemeyer, 2025 , 2026). Participation is itself endogenous, as identity-central players may select into, and stigma-sensitive players out of, a study they read as a referendum on gamers.

Crucially, the framework nests rather than replaces the established models. The GAM remains a strong withinepisode account of how person and situation inputs generate hostile cognition, affect, and arousal once an episode has been entered and framed, and the I³ framework remains the most direct account of when instigation, impellance, and low inhibition convert an aggressive impulse into an aggressive act (Step 3). What neither centrally theorizes, and what the framework supplies, is how individuals come to inhabit the enactment-relevant situation in the first place, how nominally identical situations are differently construed, how non-gameplay episodes (a relative's dismissal of gaming, a news segment linking a shooting to games) enter the causal ecology, and how layered updates produce divergent trajectories from similar baselines. The result is not a verdict for either camp but a diagnosis of why the debate has resisted resolution: both sides have often estimated an average contrast over an undifferentiated, endogenously selected, and participantconstrued exposure that is too coarse to carry the causal weight placed on it, and where boundary conditions are neither measured nor modeled, discrepant results cannot in principle be attributed to a spurious original finding rather than to unrecognized moderators (Moeller et al., 2025). The corresponding research direction is to measure episode ecologies and selection directly, and to model selection and effect as recursively coupled rather than as competitors.

Identity-Relevant Embedding and the Gaming-Addiction Literature.

Research on problematic gaming is theoretically rich, with well-developed accounts of proximal mechanism: the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution model (I-PACE; Brand et al., 2016 Brand et al., , 2019)), cue-reactivity and incentive-sensitization accounts, reinforcement models, and compensatory-coping approaches (Kardefelt-Winther, 2014). Yet several debates persist that are interpretive rather than mechanistic: distinguishing high engagement from pathology, separating addiction from coping, and making sense of measurement instability and widely varying prevalence estimates (King et al., 2020; Slack et al., 2022). These are less failures of mechanism than signs that the field's causal object and unit of analysis remain underspecified.

Our framework's leverage here comes from treating gaming as identity-relevant and socially embedded, and from the recursive carryover through which episodes accumulate into path-dependent streams. We reinterpret the phenomenon by redescribing "problematic gaming" as a recursively maintained episode ecology in which gaming becomes embedded in identity, most directly in the practice-based gamer layer of centrality, accumulated need satisfaction, and boundary salience.

Consider one of the most reproducible findings in the literature: escapism is the motive most strongly associated with gaming-disorder symptoms (pooled r ≈ .40; Wang & Cheng, 2022), with reciprocal links to internalizing distress (Amendola et al., 2025). The coping and addiction readings each treat this association as evidence for their respective positions. The framework reads it recursively. Distress repeatedly channels selection (Step 0) into episode types that deliver genuine short-term regulation but that, over cycles, strengthen gamer-identity centrality, displace alternative sources of regulation, and progressively narrow the episode ecology. In this context, the notions of "coping" and "disorder" are thereby linked through an identity-embedding history rather than opposed as mutually exclusive explanations, which is why the same behavior can be regulating in the short term and impairing over time. On the same logic, the engagementversus-pathology boundary is relocated from quantity to episode architecture: highly engaged but non-impaired players select episodes under conditions of autonomy and self-concept match and integrate them with offline life, whereas impairing patterns involve episodes increasingly selected under distress, cue pressure, and identity dependence, with recursive carryover and displacement doing the discriminating work that gaming time alone cannot (Charlton & Danforth, 2007; Slack et al., 2022).

The social embedding lens re-reads other observations as well. Cues such as notifications and group prompts can be seen as episode-entry mechanisms whose clinical meaning depends on which episodes they recruit the person into, which helps explain why cue-reactivity is real but not diagnostically specific. Apparently compulsive continuation may partly reflect social-role and gamer-identity obligation, such as being needed by a team or preserving standing, rather than hedonic compulsion alone, so that structurally different episode ecologies can produce superficially identical persistence. Measurement instability would be re-read as construct underspecification: if one nominal disorder label compresses several recursive episode patterns, instruments will capture different process bundles in different samples, and prevalence estimates will move with them (King et al., 2020). Finally, because family conflict, stigma, and intervention are themselves episodes, the framework predicts that whether an intervention helps or backfires depends on whether it is resolved through accommodation or antagonism, offering a principled account of why some pathologizing messages reduce symptoms while others harden defensive gaming.

The claim is deliberately reinterpretive. For tightly proximal questions about craving or inhibitory control, existing models remain more direct, and our framework must not be used to dissolve clinically real impairment into pure interpretation. Its contribution is to show that several stalled debates may be better understood as products of differently structured, identity-embedded episode ecologies than as uniform expressions of a single addiction process.

Episode Ecologies and Gaming-Related Radicalization.

A recent and fast-moving literature examines the intersection of gaming ecosystems and radicalization into violent extremism. Authoritative reviews frame gaming as an enabler, host, or context that can be exploited rather than as a direct cause of extremism (Council of the European Union, 2020; Public Safety Canada, 2024); however, population-level evidence is thin: online gaming was recorded for only 7% of convicted extremists in one government dataset (Kenyon et al., 2022). At the same time, documented cases show extremist actors exploiting these spaces through propaganda video games, symbolic borrowing of shooter video game aesthetics, gamified messaging, grooming in gaming-adjacent chat, and migration to platforms such as Discord (Al-Rawi, 2018; Koehler et al., 2023; Verdegaal & Wouterse, 2020; Wells et al., 2024). It can be argued that a difficulty in this line of research is that "context" and "enabler" name a relationship without specifying the psychologically active unit.

Our framework supplies that unit: the episode. It reframes the question from "do games cause extremism?" toward "how do particular gaming-related episodes become relevant to radicalization, for whom, and under what conditions?" This shifts analysis from platforms as objects to episodes as subjectively construed, and it makes construal endogeneity central, because the same chat exchange, meme, or joke may be meaningless banter for one participant, identity affirmation for another, and ideological acclimation for a third.

Read through the framework, some of the literature's important findings gain a mechanism. Koehler et al. (2023) found that the radicalization of minors was driven by organic social bonding, with ideology concentrated in Discord servers rather than in gameplay itself; our framework specifies why migration to Discord matters, namely that it changes the episode ecology from public, semi-supervised play into intimate, norm-enforcing spaces where different advisors, potencies, and opportunity structures apply. Recurrent dark humor and toxic subcultural overlap (Wells et al., 2024) are redescribed as repeated identity-relevant episodes that function as boundary testing, ingroup signaling, and gradual reclassification of what feels acceptable, which clarifies how normalization can occur without formal indoctrination and why agencies struggle to separate "joking" from genuine threat, since the same episode can serve several functions at once. Symbolic borrowing of gaming aesthetics is reread as an attempt to create episodes of recognition and fit, for example, a signal that "these people speak my cultural language," which also explains why such attempts can fail, as audiences mocked rather than embraced the ISIS propaganda game (Al-Rawi, 2018). And the vulnerability of isolated youth is re-specified: what recruiters gain access to is not merely a reachable demographic but a population for whom repeated episodes of belonging, recognition, and significance are otherwise scarce (Europol, 2022; Five Eyes/NZSIS, n.d.).

This application illustrates how the framework provides analytic precision without causing "moral panic": it explains how a platform can become radicalizationrelevant without the game being the cause, it complements rather than replaces grievance and movement-level theories, and it amplifies rather than weakens the literature's own warning against stigmatizing gaming broadly (Schlegel, 2021; Lakhani et al., 2022). Its distinctive yield is a set of researchable questions, for instance which episode distributions, understood as combinations of humor, grievance, migration, and belonging episodes, predict later risk beyond raw platform exposure, and under what conditions gamer identity becomes linked to grievance rather than buffering against it.

Practical Implications

Although this framework is not yet a completed formal theory, it identifies dimensions future research must better specify: episode selection and construal, layer-specific potency, how threat, legitimacy, and belonging security shape resolution, cross-layer coupling, and stabilization over time. The implications below are directions entailed by its logic.

Typical Exposure Designs Are Underspecified

If exposure is endogenous and loops back into future selection, designs that measure only hours played, genre, or violent content are missing the mechanism. Adequately testing the framework's claims requires measuring prior identity states, episode selection processes, salience, opportunity, discrepancy, resolution mode, and stabilization; in adjacent work on self-concept structure, a configural index of how self-representations relate to one another predicted proactive behavior over and above the established single-dimension measure of how salient and easily imagined those representations are (Strauss et al., 2026). Without such measurement, studies risk collapsing antecedents, mediators, and outcomes into a single undifferentiated "effect of video games."

The framework also implies tracking episode streams longitudinally, separating within-person change from between-person differences, and treating post-episode identity as the next episode's starting condition, although separating the two levels is necessary rather than sufficient, because the within-person coefficient a multilevel model returns is itself a between-person aggregate (Baars et al., 2025). Dynamic, repeated-measures approaches are more appropriate than one-shot designs if the goal is to test the model's recursive structure rather than merely detect associations. Two participants with equal playtime are not necessarily comparable: they may have entered different episode ecologies with different opportunity structures and different identity stakes. Total gaming time is therefore a poor proxy for psychologically meaningful exposure.

Because whether a situation qualifies as an episode is partly constituted by participant construal, even externally coded episode types may be insufficient. Researchers would need to measure whether gaming-related meaning was activated, which identity layers were implicated, and what cues triggered the association. The practical exposure construct thus shifts toward gaming-relevant episode density or frequency of gaming-linked construals across contexts, not simply play frequency. Idiographic and experience-sampling methods (event-contingent diaries, ecological momentary assessment, qualitative or mixedmethod event reconstruction) therefore become more important, because only the participant can report whether a seemingly ordinary event became gaming-relevant in their own processing. This favors emic measurement, in which items are selected or generated for the individual rather than imported from a population-level instrument, and event-contingent sampling, which is indicated when the situations of interest occur too rarely for intervalcontingent prompts to capture them (Kuper et al., 2025).

Selection Must Be Modeled Explicitly

Because Step 0 is the framework's explicit mechanism for endogeneity, selection cannot be treated as background noise. Studies would need to measure motives, self-concept match, group obligations, exploratory intent, habit, access constraints, and expected payoff, because these determine what enters the person's episode-based experience in the first place. Failure to model selection risks misattributing identity-driven self-selection effects to causal influences of gaming itself.

A related concern is that if gaming-derived semantic traces can be activated outside explicitly gaming contexts, experimental control conditions are less clean than they appear. A nominally non-gaming task may still be processed through gamer identity, competition scripts, mastery schemas, stigma sensitivity, or narrative frames for some participants. The salience-opportunity distinction implies that identity can matter even when the context is not overtly about gaming, so measuring prior gamer identity, gaming-derived meanings, and situational construal is necessary to avoid hidden contamination of supposedly neutral conditions.

Resolution Conditions and the Role of Public Discourse

A practical implication of considerable applied significance is that changing the content of an episode may matter less than changing whether it is processed through accommodation, assimilation, or antagonism. Accommodation is most likely when perceived threat is manageable, legitimacy of the feedback source is high, and belonging security is intact, a source condition consistent with evidence that identity validation carries weight in proportion to the audience's status, task interdependence, power, and knowledge of the identity being enacted (Ashforth & Schinoff, 2016); antagonism is favored when threat is high, legitimacy is low, and belonging security is precarious.

This has direct consequences for how gaming-related concerns are communicated. If the goal is constructive change, criticism of gaming or gamers should be credible, specific, fair, and delivered in contexts where updating does not imply humiliation or exclusion. Public caricature, contempt, or sweeping moral accusation often produces the opposite of the intended effect, strengthening defensive gamer identity rather than revising beliefs or behavior. Outsiders who discuss gamers in devaluing ways may be contributing to the defensive boundary hardening they later observe. Respectful, informed engagement increases the probability that identity-relevant discrepancies are treated as credible and safe to integrate.

Family discourse, journalistic framing, institutional rhetoric, and scientific communication are not external commentary on gaming; they are part of the causal system. These contexts can instantiate gaming-relevant episodes whenever they activate gamer identity, cultural meaning, legitimacy concerns, or boundary salience. The recursive loop does not require gameplay to keep operating; it can be sustained through the symbolic and social environments in which gaming-related meanings circulate. Any blanket recommendation about "the effects of gaming" is therefore practically incomplete: the same platform rule or public message may produce learning in one subgroup, null effects in another, and defensive escalation in a third, depending on identity centrality, opportunity structure, threat, and prior episode history. Subgroup structure of this kind is documented empirically elsewhere, where the distribution of within-person associations across people is often multimodal, and positive, negative, and null associations for the same pair of variables coexist within a single sample (Baars et al., 2025). Efforts to address gaming-related outcomes should therefore be stratified by episode ecology and identity configuration, not only by content category.

Participation in Video Game Research as an Episode

A particularly consequential implication concerns the research process itself. Participation in a study about video games is rarely a neutral observation context: it is frequently an out-of-game episode in its own right, because out-of-game episodes are defined as real-life encounters that activate gaming-related episodic memory or semantic knowledge. A study whose title, consent form, instructions, measures, or task content makes gaming salient, or that feels like an evaluation of gaming or of the participant as a gamer, becomes part of the causal system rather than sitting outside it.

In a research setting, Step 1 implies that participants rapidly construct a working interpretation of the episode. They may frame the study as a neutral survey, a scientific attempt to understand gaming, a judgment of gamers, an opportunity to represent gamers fairly, or a context reflecting negative assumptions about gaming. These framings are not epiphenomenal: they determine what becomes salient evidence, which identity advisors carry greater influence, and which response tendencies are activated in Step 3. Once gamer salience is active, behavior inside the study can be partly produced by the practice-based gamer advisor: identity-protective responding, selective candor, norm signaling, stereotype resistance, or attempts to present gaming in a particular light.

Step 2 also has practical implications: if a participant interprets a study as evaluative, stereotype-relevant, or tied to how gamers are publicly perceived, it becomes a higher-potency episode than a routine survey, increasing the probability of genuine identity-relevant processing (including defensive processing) rather than mechanical responding. The measured outcome may then reflect a compound of the substantive manipulation and the identityshaped processing triggered by the study context. This is more specific than ordinary demand characteristics: the study may instantiate a practice-based gamer episode in which the framework's recursive machinery operates on the research context.

These implications are especially strong for research on controversial topics such as violent video games and aggression: participants who identify as gamers may enter a study about "the effects of violent video games" already in identity-defensive mode, treating the study as part of an ongoing public debate about gamers as a category. The framework predicts that under such conditions, results may reflect not only the manipulated variable but also the appraisal and resolution dynamics activated by participation itself.

Two qualifications are necessary. First, the framework does not imply that every video game study is automatically invalid; whether identity processing is engaged depends on whether gamer identity becomes salient under the study's conditions. Studies of basic perceptual or cognitive performance using narrowly defined tasks may approximate the conditions for individual-level treatment effects when participants are unlikely to enter the task in identity-protective mode; a comparable gradient has been proposed for experimental psychology at large, with failures of group-to-person generalizability expected to be more likely in higher-level social cognition than in perception (McManus et al., 2023). The framework's critique applies most strongly when the outcome of interest is itself identity-relevant (aggression, attitudes, social judgments, narrative interpretation, moral reasoning). Second, identity processing during research participation is not a flaw to be eliminated but a phenomenon to be modeled: under the framework, what participants do in a study is partly a function of the participation episode itself, and effects estimated under controlled conditions are estimates of how identity-mediated processing operates under those specific framing, salience, and opportunity conditions, not invariant effects of "video game exposure."

Step 0 also implies that if a study is visibly about gaming, participation itself may already be endogenous. Some people select in because they identify as gamers, want their perspective represented, or wish to defend gaming; others select out because they anticipate stigma, distrust the framing, or expect bias. The sample is then partly people who entered a gaming-adjacent episode for identityshaped reasons, further complicating causal estimation from video game studies: when both the causal variable and the outcome raise the probability of taking part, study participation becomes a collider, and the resulting bias operates without any explicit statistical control (Bailey et al., 2024).

Developmental Sensitivity

The framework is compatible with the view that gaming during adolescence and early adulthood may have disproportionate developmental leverage, because personal identity is relatively more exploratory and consolidating during those periods. If early episodes are potent, emotionally meaningful, repeated, and consolidated, they can set the starting conditions for subsequent cycles, producing substantial downstream effects through path-dependent accumulation. The model is nonetheless recursive and lifespan-compatible: identity is updated across repeated episodes throughout life, and substantial later updating remains possible, especially for social, cultural, and gamer identity, when episodes are high in potency, salience, public consequence, and emotional meaning, a structure that parallels accounts in which entry into a new setting is the period of greatest malleability while construction and re-construction can be retriggered at any later point by identity threats, surprises, and disruptive or critical events (Ashforth & Schinoff, 2016).

The carryover identity state entering any gaming episode is not shaped exclusively by prior gaming; family, school, peers, other media, and broader cultural experiences contribute to the identity layers present when an episode begins, and these external streams can themselves become sites of gaming-relevant feedback when they activate gaming-related meaning. During developmentally sensitive periods, gaming may be one particularly potent stream among others, but its long-term influence depends on whether gaming-related episodes repeatedly generate discrepancy signals that are resolved through accommodation or antagonism rather than assimilation.

Toward an Empirical Agenda

The purpose of our framework is to specify a process architecture and identify empirical questions, and future work should therefore proceed in stages.

The agenda has three interlocking tasks. A descriptive task: map the ecology of gaming-relevant episodes people encounter and how those episodes are subjectively construed, including how often the same objective event is coded as gaming-relevant by different people. A mechanistic task: identify the cues and conditions that shape layer-specific salience, anticipated and realized potency, advisor weighting, resolution mode, cross-layer coupling, and the conditions under which threat combined with low legitimacy produces antagonism rather than assimilation. A developmental task: test whether repeated episode streams produce the predicted path-dependent and nonlinear trajectories, using repeated-measures or diary designs, multilevel within-person modeling, person-specific or subgroup trajectory models, and designs that model selection into episode streams rather than treating exposure as exogenous. Because a sample-level within-person estimate is itself an aggregate across people, this task also requires testing whether a single within-person pattern in fact fits all participants rather than assuming that it does, for which explicit procedures now exist (Baars et al., 2025).

The framework is therefore intended less as a final account than as a structured agenda: its value lies in identifying the right questions and specifying the architecture within which they can be addressed. On a Lakatosian criterion, a program of this kind earns its standing only insofar as successive specifications of boundary conditions yield new predictions rather than post hoc accommodation of discrepant results (Moeller et al., 2025).

Falsifiable Predictions

Although the present framework is not yet a formalized computational model, it yields explicit empirical predictions: episode effects should be layer-specific rather than globally uniform; identity updating should be better explained by layer-specific potency and resolution conditions than by exposure alone; prior identity states should shape later episode selection; and aligned cross-layer updates should predict stronger consolidation than misaligned ones.

These predictions provide clear points at which the framework can be refined, revised, or rejected. A non-exhaustive but detailed set of falsifiable predictions, organized by the framework's core mechanisms, is provided in Supplementary Material 6 on the OSF repository. Full bibliographic entries for the video games named in this paper and its supplementary materials are listed separately in Supplementary Material 7.

Conclusion

This paper has set out to reconceptualize how gaming is theorized in psychological research, moving from a linear exposure framework to a dynamic, identity-centered one. The integrative episode-based framework treats gaming and identity as mutually constitutive across repeated episodes, specifying the recursive cycle through which identities shape episode selection, framing, and behavior, while episodes generate layered feedback that is appraised, resolved, and selectively stabilized into durable carryover states. Whether a situation constitutes a gamingrelevant episode is partly determined by participant construal, making exposure endogenous at two levels: selection into situations and interpretation of those situations as gaming-relevant. Effects are layered across four identity layers that can be updated in parallel, yielding internally mixed profiles, and change depends on discrepancy plus resolution conditions shaped by threat, legitimacy, and belonging security. These features produce path-dependent, nonlinear trajectories in which heterogeneity is predicted rather than residual.

The framework carries substantial implications for research practice, though these should be read as entailments of its process logic rather than prescriptions presupposing full operational readiness. Standard exposure designs are underspecified relative to the recursive, endogenous, multi-layered process described. Future research would benefit from modeling selection and carryover states explicitly, measuring subjective construal rather than relying on external event categories, and adopting dynamic repeated-measures designs capable of tracking recursive within-person processes. Public discourse, family communication, institutional rhetoric, and the research process itself enter the causal system rather than standing outside it, and blanket recommendations about the effects of gaming are rendered implausible by a framework predicting fundamentally different outcomes depending on identity centrality, episode ecology, resolution conditions, and prior trajectory. Because public communication about gaming belongs to that system, Supplementary Material 8 restates the framework in nontechnical terms for a general readership.

More broadly, understood as a theoretical scaffold and empirical agenda rather than a finalized formal model, the framework invites a shift in how we think about what video games are in the context of identity development. They are not inert stimuli acting upon passive recipients. They are arenas in which people explore who they are, negotiate who they belong to, defend what they value, and gradually become who they will be. The recursive loops described do not begin and end with a play session: they travel through memory, meaning, and social life, quietly shaping how the world is seen long after the screen is turned off. If video game research is to keep pace with what gaming has become, it must begin from the recogni-tion that video games are not simply producers of effects. They are part of the architecture through which people interpret and construct who they are. key Kong (Nintendo R&D1, 1981) and Grand Theft Auto III (DMA Design, 2001), to make concrete the argument that the object denoted by the term "video games" has changed substantially over time. Panels A and C are in-game screenshots; Panels B and D are schematic representations of the corresponding gameplay affordances, so that the perceptual and interactive demands of each title can be compared directly.

Panels A and B characterize Donkey Kong, an early platformer representative of arcade-era design. As the screenshot in Panel A shows, the player occupies a limited twodimensional space, navigating ladders and platforms while avoiding a small set of scripted hazards.
