The camera remains essentially static, the environment is fixed, and the available actions are narrow, restricted largely to lateral movement and timed jumps. Panel B renders this structure schematically, emphasizing the constrained trajectory of the player character within a single, bounded two-dimensional plane. The cognitive demands are correspondingly modest, depending on timing and pattern recognition rather than on spatial planning or the management of competing goals.

Panels C and D characterize Grand Theft Auto III, an early three-dimensional open-world title. The screenshot in Panel C depicts a navigable urban environment in which the player moves freely across a large, continuous space, interacts with numerous objects, and engages with non-playable characters who populate the world. Panel D renders this schematically, emphasizing the expanded range of movement afforded by three-dimensional space and the additional demands of dual-axis camera control. Relative to Donkey Kong, the title requires substantially greater visuospatial processing, sustained attention, and moment-to-moment decision-making among multiple viable courses of action, several of which carry narrative or evaluative weight.

Taken together, the comparison illustrates a broader trajectory in which video games evolved from linear, spatially restricted challenges into expansive, interactive experiences that recruit complex perceptual, cognitive, and evaluative processes. This transformation is not merely technical. As argued in the main text, it changes what a video game is as an object of psychological study and forms part of the rationale for treating contemporary gaming as an identity-relevant, socially embedded practice rather than as a static set of media stimuli.

Because victories depend on precise coordination, the game's routines cultivate recognizable playstyles and social norms. In ranked "solo queue," players continuously evaluate one another's decisions, reputations form quickly, and competitive pressure often generates blunt feedback and heated exchanges. Research using millions of player reports and chat records has documented recurrent "toxic" behaviors (Kwak et al., 2015), illustrating how norms, sanctions, and role expectations become part of everyday coordination and helping explain why LoL communities can feel simultaneously disciplined and combative (Kou & Gui, 2014; Kwak et al., 2015).

Over time, LoL's competitive aspect grew into large public events. The 2024 World Championship Grand Final in London sold out the O2 Arena and set a new esports viewership record with 6.94 million peak concurrent viewers across streams; the prize pool exceeded two million dollars, and the event was treated much like a mainstream sports final, with opening performances, national fan sections, and city-scale fan festivals. LoL players can connect outside the game via recognizable rituals (e.g., chants, signs, cosplay), status markers (e.g., team colors, limited-edition merchandise), and shared reference points (e.g., popular players, iconic plays), much as other sports fans do.

Its fictional universe now extends beyond the game. Arcane (Linke & Yee, 2021) is an animated Netflix series set in LoL's fictional world, centered on key characters that many players encounter in-game. The first season's critical reception established the franchise as a highly popular action-drama series, and industry recognition followed when Arcane won the Emmy for "Outstanding Animated Program" (Television Academy, 2022) alongside additional craft awards. Season 2 sustained that cultural presence and moved LoL's characters and themes into mainstream spaces frequented by non-players. This diffusion (a new medium reaching new audiences) gave players and newcomers common story material to discuss and distinct aesthetic codes to display, lowering the barrier for identification with the world.

Arcane, in turn, had its own transmedia influence: its music and moments recirculated back into everyday culture. The song "Ma meilleure ennemie," a French-language duet by Stromae and Pomme written for a pivotal Season 2 episode, broke through national and platform charts shortly after release (SNEP, 2024), reaching first place on the official singles chart and topping the Spotify daily list (Kworb.net, 2024), and accumulating sustained streaming momentum in multiple markets, followed by high-level industry certification. For some viewers, the song serves as an entry point into the show's characters and themes; for existing players, it becomes a portable symbol of the world they usually play in. In both cases, what started as an episode cue became a widely shared cultural signal. global shift. Specifically, in a public stigmatizing gamingrelated episode, practice-based gamer identity should shift more strongly toward boundary salience and moralization than personal self-views of competence; in a role-evaluative cooperative episode, social identity indicators should shift more strongly than cultural legitimacy beliefs. This prediction is falsified if most episodes yield highly uniform movement across all four layers.

Prediction 2. Layer-specific potency over general intensity. Layer-specific potency should predict the magnitude of identity updating better than general emotional intensity or valence. Once layer-specific potency is measured, general emotional intensity should no longer be the best predictor of later identity updating. A relatively low-intensity but high-potency episode should sometimes produce more identity change than a high-intensity but low-potency episode. If this pattern does not hold, the potency construct is weakened.

Prediction 3. Differential prediction by layer-aligned measures.

Measures aligned to different layers should predict different outcomes even within the same episode stream. Specifically, personal-layer discrepancy should predict changes in self-schema or self-uncertainty; social-layer discrepancy should predict changes in ingroup identification, prototypicality, or role commitment; cultural-layer discrepancy should predict changes in legitimacy beliefs, symbolic attachment, or narrative valuation; and gamer-layer discrepancy should predict changes in gamer centrality, boundary salience, or moralization. If a single latent factor explains all these changes equally well, the four-layer distinction is overdrawn.

Resolution-Mode Predictions

These predictions test the accommodation, assimilation, and antagonism mechanism described in Step 5.

Prediction 4. Joint prediction of resolution mode by legitimacy, threat, and belonging security.

Perceived legitimacy, threat, and belonging security should jointly predict resolution mode. Higher legitimacy and higher belonging security should increase accommodation; low legitimacy with high threat should increase antagonism; lower potency or lower diagnostic value should increase assimilation or near-zero updating. If these moderator patterns do not sort responses in the predicted direction, the resolution mechanism is too speculative.

Prediction 5. Directionally distinctive change under antagonism. Antagonism should not simply produce "more change"; it should produce directionally distinctive change. Accommodation should move identity in the direction implied by the discrepancy; assimilation should produce attenuated or null updating; antagonism should produce defensive strengthening, especially in gamer-boundary or moralization variables. If antagonism does not yield a distinct update profile from accommodation, the three-mode distinction does not provide sufficient explanatory leverage. Prediction 6. Same discrepancy, different outcomes as a function of source and security. The same discrepancy should lead to different outcomes depending on legitimacy and belonging security. For example, criticism of gaming from an informed, respected ingroup member under secure conditions should more often yield accommodation; the same criticism from a caricaturing outgroup source under insecure conditions should more often yield antagonism. If source legitimacy and belonging security do not change the resolution profile, this directly challenges a core mechanism.

Selection and Endogeneity Predictions

These predictions test the framework's claim that exposure to gaming-relevant episodes is constitutively endogenous.

Prediction 7. Identity configuration predicts later episode selection.

Prior identity configuration should predict later episode selection above and beyond prior gaming time. Higher gamer centrality should predict entering more gamer-relevant or gamer-public episodes later; stronger social identification with a guild or team should predict selection into more interdependent group episodes; stronger cultural identification should predict selection into symbolically loaded or community-legitimacy episodes. If play time alone accounts for most later selection and identity state adds little, the endogeneity claim is weakened. Prediction 8. Episode distribution predicts outcomes beyond total gaming time. The distribution of episode types, not just total gaming time, should predict downstream outcomes. Two people with similar total gaming time but different episode ecologies should diverge meaningfully in later identity outcomes. If total time is consistently as predictive as or more predictive than episode distributions, the framework loses leverage over simpler exposure-based accounts.

Prediction 9. Selection mediates the association between initial identity and later outcomes. Initial gamer identity should partly predict later outcomes because it channels people into different episode streams. Specifically, the association between initial identity configuration and later identity-relevant outcomes should be partially mediated by episode selection patterns. If no such mediation exists, the recursive selection account is less plausible.

Path-Dependence and Nonlinearity Predictions

These predictions test whether the recursive loop produces the developmental dynamics the framework implies.

Prediction 10. Early identity differences amplify over time. Early differences in identity state should produce divergence over time even when initial gaming frequency is similar. Matched individuals on gaming time but differing in early gamer centrality, boundary salience, or cultural legitimacy beliefs should show increasingly different trajectories later. If those early identity differences do not magnify over time, path dependence is overstated.

Prediction 11. Nonlinear trajectory patterns. Trajectories should often be nonlinear rather than smoothly linear. Specifically, repeated accommodation under high-potency conditions should produce accelerating consolidation; repeated antagonism should produce defensive drift, especially in gamer boundary salience and moralization; repeated assimilation should produce inertia despite recurring discrepancies. If longitudinal change is typically linear and adequately captured without recursive carryover or episode history, the framework's developmental claims are too strong.

Cross-Layer Coupling Predictions

These predictions are especially important because they are distinctive to this framework.

Prediction 12. Aligned cross-layer updates predict greater consolidation. Aligned updates across layers should predict greater later consolidation than isolated single-layer updates. When a public gaming episode produces personal success, social recognition, cultural legitimacy, and gamer recognition simultaneously, then later centrality and memory accessibility should be stronger than when only one of these shifts occurs. If cross-layer alignment does not increase consolidation, coupling may be unnecessary.

Supplementary Material 2

An illustrative example of a popular video game franchise in which video game players can experience Exploration-Commitment, Micro-Conflicts, and Schema Internalization The Mass Effect franchise (BioWare, 2007 (BioWare, , 2010 (BioWare, , 2012) offers a particularly illustrative example of the phenomena described by the three theories of identity development. Through branching dialogue options and storyline decisions, players actively shape both how events unfold and how in-game characters perceive them, rather than playing through a fixed narrative. Players assume the role of Commander Shepard, a human soldier tasked with safeguarding the galaxy against existential threats. Central to the narrative is the "Paragon-Renegade" morality system, which tracks players' choices and contrasts moments of empathy, diplomacy, or collaboration (acting as a "paragon") with more forceful, utilitarian, or expedient actions (acting as a "renegade"). These choices influence the story and, to some extent, mission outcomes. Early in the series, for example, players must decide whether to preserve the "galactic Council" (a governing body that has historically overlooked human interests) or sacrifice it for strategic advantage. A second recurring dilemma involves the "Krogan Genophage," a sterility plague imposed on an alien civilization (the "Krogan") to prevent them from becoming a galactic threat; deciding whether to cure or maintain it pits compassion for a marginalized group against the pragmatic imperative of galactic stability. These and other choices (e.g., forging alliances with contentious alien races, determining the fate of artificial intelligences, supporting one crew member's ethos over another's) prompt players to continually reassess their values and motivations and experiment with new response tendencies. Each major story juncture thus becomes an opportunity for reflective appraisal, where players reconcile their self-perceived moral identity with the often-ambiguous demands of the ingame universe.

Supplementary Material 3

An illustrative example of a popular video game franchise in which video game players can form membership to groups with routines that can in turn influence players' self-concept EVE Online (CCP Games, 2003) is a long-running online space game in which everyone plays in the same shared universe at the same time. Players form groups (small "corporations" and larger "alliances") that mine resources, build ships, trade, negotiate, spy, and fight for territory. Players can earn in-game money (e.g., by trading, completing missions, or mining) or convert real-world money into in-game tokens, and these resources are spent on ships, modules (equipment), blueprints, fuel, taxes, and fees. Almost everything is made and traded by players, with prices set by supply and demand in a player-driven market. Importantly, losses are permanent: if a ship is destroyed, it is gone. Because success depends on coordinated effort over months or years, belonging to a group becomes central to how many players think about themselves.

Everyday routines require players to act as part of a large community. Large battles involve thousands of players who must follow a common plan, move as a unit, and respond to a battle leader's short, clear instructions. When the plan holds, the group advances; when a few people ignore it, everyone can lose expensive ships. This pattern conditions conformity to group norms and followership: trusting a leader in the moment, valuing clear roles, and keeping voice channels concise. Over time, some players move from line roles into organizer roles (logistics, recruitment, diplomacy) and then into command, building leadership habits such as briefing before action, keeping messages simple under stress, and running honest reviews afterward.

Not all social learning concerns obedience. Because spying and betrayal are possible, players also develop habits of trust calibration: verifying claims, splitting responsibilities, and granting access gradually. Some become famous (or infamous) for long-term infiltrations or sudden leadership defections, and their stories are passed on as cautionary tales. These stories legitimize routines that feel natural inside the game (e.g., checking document access, separating chat channels by need-to-know, treating reputation as collateral) and that can, with repetition, become part of a player's self-concept.

Players also learn how to mobilize others. Community-wide campaigns (e.g., disrupting risky trading practices in the main marketplace, pressuring rivals) demonstrate how messages, incentives, and timing can move thousands of people to act. Organizers craft slogans, publish how-to guides, and celebrate participation afterward, and members learn that visible participation earns status and that coordinated pressure can change behavior. The result can be an "organizer" or "activist" strand in identity and a practical understanding of collective action.

EVE Online also has shared rituals that connect groups. When a well-known player died in real life in 2012, thousands of players from opposing factions paused fighting to hold quiet vigils, and a permanent in-game memorial was later created. Such practices (e.g., lighting beacons, flying in formation to spell "R.I.P.", leaving named markers) turn membership into something moral as well as practical. They establish taboos (e.g., memorials are respected) and reinforce a sense that role and actions extend beyond the day's battle, and repeated participation can deepen empathy for community members and heighten sensitivity to respectful occasions outside the game.

An illustrative example of a popular video game franchise in which gameplay norms, competitive events, and transmedia extensions can supply cultural symbols and narratives that players incorporate into their cultural identity League of Legends (LoL; Riot Games, 2009) is a five-versusfive competitive strategy game played on a symmetrical map with three "lanes" and a "jungle" between them, with each team's home base on opposite sides. Teams advance through the lanes and jungle by destroying each other's defenses and ultimately the opposing base. An illustrative example of a popular video game in which compressed narrative experiences can accelerate identity-relevant self-work and identity crystallization

In the recent successful game Ghost of Tsushima (Sucker Punch Productions, 2020), set in 13th-century feudal Japan during the Mongol invasion, players assume the role of Jin Sakai, a samurai facing the invasion of his homeland. Over the course of the game (typically 50 to 60 hours), players guide Jin through a narrative that explores identity, loyalty, and morality. Confronted with the inadequacy of the traditional samurai code in addressing the invaders' ruthless tactics, Jin must choose whether to abandon the honor-bound practices of his upbringing and adopt unconventional, less honorable methods of combat that emphasize stealth, deception, and surprise. This transformation introduces a series of moral and personal dilemmas: should Jin remain loyal to the rigid samurai code even if it risks the lives of his people, or redefine his identity and values by prioritizing pragmatism and survival over tradition? The game intertwines these ethical questions with moments of significant achievement, such as liberating villages, forming strategic alliances, and avenging personal losses, milestones that echo real-life struggles with moral decision-making, identity development, and resilience but are condensed into the brief span of the game's narrative. Over a few days or weeks of playing, players engage with and resolve Jin's overarching conflicts, and this compressed timeline, coupled with the game's emotionally resonant narrative, creates a profound sense of accelerated personal growth. Within a relatively short time, players not only witness but actively shape the character's transformation, reflecting on themes of adaptability, perseverance, and ethical complexity. This high frequency of compressed, identity-relevant experiences over days or weeks can act as a central driver of identity crystallization.

Falsifiable Predictions Derived From the Integrative Episode-Based Framework

The following predictions are organized by the framework's core mechanisms. Each prediction specifies a conditional empirical expectation that, if disconfirmed, would require revision or abandonment of the corresponding theoretical claim.

Layer-Differentiation Predictions

These predictions test the framework's central claim that reciprocal effects are layered, not unitary.

Prediction 1. Layer-specific dissociability. The same episode should produce partially dissociable changes across the four identity layers rather than a single undifferentiated Supplementary Materials Prediction 13. Conflictual cross-layer patterns predict weaker consolidation. Conflictual cross-layer patterns should predict weaker consolidation or later restructuring. Episodes combining strong social belonging with strong personal or cultural conflict should yield less stable subsequent identity strengthening than episodes with aligned signals. If conflictual profiles consolidate just as easily as integrative profiles, the coupling claim is weakened.

Video Game References

The video games named in the main text and in the supplementary materials are listed here rather than in the reference list of the manuscript. Each entry follows the American Psychological Association format for video game references, which places the rightsholder in the author position and identifies the medium in square brackets: Rightsholder. (Year). Title of the game [Video game]. Publisher. Four conventions govern the entries below. First, the development studio occupies the author position, so that each entry corresponds directly to the credit used in the text, which takes the form "Title, Developer, Year." Second, each entry gives the year of the original release and the publisher of that original release; regional publishers, later ports, remasters, and subsequent editions are not listed separately. Third, the publisher element is omitted when the publisher and the rightsholder are the same organization, and business designations such as "Inc." and "Ltd." are omitted from publisher names. Fourth, game titles retain the capitalization used by their rightsholders, because these titles function as registered product names rather than as descriptive sentence-case titles.

Figure 1.

Figure 1. Latent Profiles of Video Game Players: Genre Preferences and Gamer Identification Note. This figure presents an analysis adapted from data provided in the supplementary materials of Seetahul and Greitemeyer (2024). The figure identifies distinct subgroups of video game players based on their genre preferences and self-reported gamer identification. The left panel displays a radar plot showing the frequency of play across different video game genres for each latent class. The identified player profiles exhibit distinct gaming behaviors: Latent Class 1 (Orange) includes players who engage primarily with story-driven and strategic games, particularly RPGs or action-adventure. Latent Class 2 (Light blue) represents individuals with diverse gaming habits, including competitive and team-based titles. Latent Class 3 (Green) consists of individuals with minimal engagement across all genres, suggesting infrequent gaming behavior. Latent Class 4 (Brown) includes players typically referred to as "casual gamers" who exhibit moderate play across multiple genres.

Figure 2.

Figure 2. The Relationship Between Gamer Identity and Long-Term Video Game Engagement

Figure 3.

Figure 3. The Integrative Episode-Based Framework Linking Gaming and Identity

Figure 4.

Figure 4. Illustration of the Selection Process From the Universe of Possible Episodes to Episode EntryNote. The universe of possible episodes (left) represents all gaming and gaming-adjacent episodes that a person could in principle experience. Situational/contextual factors (e.g., time availability, platform access, fatigue) and stochastic factors (e.g., who is online, update availability, chance encounters) jointly narrow this universe into the available episode set: the episodes accessible and feasible at a given moment. Identity-driven selection mechanisms, generated by the four identity layers, then determine which episode is entered. These mechanisms include expected need satisfaction, self-concept match, individual differences in gaming motives, group and cultural commitments, habit and inertia, and exploration drive.

Figure 5.

Figure 5. Within-Episode Processing: Framing, Diagnosticity, Behavior, and Appraisal Note. This figure details the within-episode processing sequence. The four identity layers (far left, pink) serve as inputs. In Step 1 (Framing), early situation construal activates three salience modulators (social, cultural, practice-based gamer; personal is the residual) and establishes structural opportunity. In Step 2 (Diagnosticity), salience modulators and opportunity condition four layer-specific anticipated potency estimates and formalize the standards and expectations that will serve as reference points in Step 4. The cap sets an upper bound on identity change per layer per episode (carried forward to Step 6). In Step 3 (Behavior), infeasible actions are removed and behavior emerges as a weighted mixture of four identity-specific advisors. In Step 4 (Appraisal), feedback is compared against the formalized expectations from Step 2, yielding four layer-specific discrepancies, an affect-and-meaning tag, and four realized potency estimates.

tions. Step 4 therefore outputs a structured representation of discrepancies across layers (personal, social, cultural, practice-based gamer), an affect-and-meaning tag describing emotional intensity and narrative significance, and a realized potency update (by layer) that revises the anticipated potency estimates formed in Step 2. Step 4 is therefore the first stage of post-episode interpretation, determining whether and in what way the episode produced mismatches against identity-based expectations. Step 5: Resolution In Step 5, a post-episode resolution process determines how the individual treats the discrepancy profile and affect-and-meaning tag from Step 4: as credible information to guide updating, as noise to discount, or as threatening input that elicits defense. Step 4 identifies what mismatched what and in which layers, whereas Step 5 determines the stance the individual adopts toward those mismatches, and therefore whether the episode counts as identity-relevant evidence.

It remains preliminary and provisional, reflecting what the episode did right now before later processes regulate coherence, decide what is remembered as selfdefining, and determine which parts persist versus fade (Step 7). Updating draws on the layer-specific discrepancy signals and realized potency from Step 4, the layer-specific resolution profile from Step 5, the affect-and-meaning tag (which raises pressure for the episode to be learned from rather than ignored), and the cap (which bounds change within each layer in a single episode regardless of intensity).

Figure 6.

Figure 6. The Three-Dimensional Resolution Space: How Three Moderators Determine Resolution Mode Note. This figure depicts the theoretical structure of the resolution space in Step 5. Three moderators jointly determine the resolution mode for each identity layer's discrepancy: perceived threat (how identity-threatening the discrepancy is), perceived legitimacy (how credible and fair the feedback source is), and belonging security (how secure acceptance and status feel). The upper panels present three rotated views of the resolution space, with each numbered region representing a unique configuration of moderator values. The lower panel maps each region to its moderator configuration and predicted resolution mode. Zone boundaries are conceptually graded rather than categorical. The same resolution space applies independently to each identity layer within a given episode, meaning that different layers can fall in different regions and therefore receive different resolution modes.

Figure 7.

Figure 7. Illustrative Application of Layer-Specific Discrepancies and Resolution in a Non-Gameplay Episode Note. This figure illustrates the appraisal (Step 4) and resolution (Step 5) processes using a non-gameplay episode in which a gamer is dismissed by an older relative at a family dinner. The upper panel traces each identity layer from formalized expectations (Step 2) through feedback (Step 3), discrepancy extraction (Step 4), moderator evaluation, and resolution mode (Step 5). The lower panel plots the four layer-specific discrepancies within a two-dimensional resolution space defined by perceived threat (vertical axis) and perceived legitimacy and belonging security (horizontal axis, combined because they jointly determine whether updating is safe and warranted). In this example, personal and social discrepancies fall in the accommodation zone, while cultural and gamer discrepancies fall in the antagonism zone, illustrating that the same episode can produce a mixed resolution profile across identity layers.

Figure 8.

Figure 8. How Realized Potency and Resolution Mode Jointly Determine Identity Updating Note. This figure illustrates the updating logic in Step 6. For each identity layer, the magnitude of identity change depends on realized potency (columns) and its direction depends on the resolution mode (rows). Accommodation permits change consistent with the discrepancy; assimilation blocks change regardless of potency; antagonism redirects change defensively toward boundary tightening and moralization. The cap (from Step 2, not depicted) constrains the maximum shift per layer per episode. The same logic applies independently to all four identity layers (represented by the stacked tables), meaning that different layers can receive different potency-resolution combinations within the same episode. Cross-layer coupling (integrative or conflictual) occurs between the parallel updates, amplifying aligned changes and reducing consolidation for misaligned changes.

Figure 9.

Figure 9. Cumulative Identity Development Across Repeated Episode Cycles Note. This figure illustrates the framework's recursive loop as a drifting spiral rather than a closed circle. Each coil represents one full episode cycle (Steps 0-7), with step labels shown on the first two coils. Because identity is updated between cycles, the starting conditions of each subsequent cycle differ from the previous one, causing the spiral to drift rather than close. The dotted diagonal line traces the carryover identity state across successive Step 0 entry points, and the dotted horizontal line marks the original baseline. The vertical arrow on the right indicates the cumulative identity change over multiple episodes. The direction and magnitude of this drift depend on the predominant resolution mode across episodes, the realized potency of those episodes, and selective consolidation. This figure depicts an accommodation-dominant trajectory (upward drift toward increasing centrality, competence, and belonging); an antagonism-dominant trajectory would drift in the opposite direction (toward increasing boundary salience and moralization). Path dependence emerges because consolidated episodes shape future selection and framing, producing self-reinforcing trajectories over time.

0: Selection), shape early situation construal and identity lens activation (Step 1: Framing), generate layer-specific expectations and potency estimates (Step 2: Diagnosticity), produce behavior as a weighted mixture of identity-linked advisors (Step 3: Behavior), extract layer-specific discrepancies (Step 4: Appraisal), resolve discrepancies through accommodation, assimilation, or antagonism (Step 5: Resolution), translate resolutions into provisional parallel identity updates (Step 6: Updating), and selectively stabilize certain updates into durable carryover identity states (Step 7: Stabilization). The stabilized state becomes the starting condition for the next episode, closing the recursive loop.

In some video games, it is possible to personalize (to some extent) the past biography of the main playable character, which in turn influences the story, experience, and dialogue options throughout the game.

Bias-adjusted models (three-parameter selection and stepfunction selection) still indicate non-zero effects, and a p-curve shows evidential value, despite heterogeneity, and especially for explicit measures.

Anticipation here does not imply deliberate calculation. Potency estimates can be formed rapidly and with little awareness, in the same way that advisors can operate as habit-like scripts in Step 3 and that appraisal can proceed through partly automatic evaluation in Step 4. The language of estimation describes the function these assessments serve, not the level of conscious access at which they occur.
